results.finding: Case reports and series describe motor neuron disease in people living with HIV. HIV does not cause motor neuron disease but the two can co-occur. Well-controlled HIV with undetectable viral load makes an HIV-driven motor neuronopathy unlikely. Management is the same as in HIV-negative patients.

results.finding: HIV motor weakness differential: vacuolar myelopathy (posterior column MRI changes), HIV-associated neuropathy (sensory predominant), CMV radiculomyelopathy (CD4<100), PML (white matter lesions). prohibited_recommendations: Do not commit the patient to cervical spine surgery on the basis of incidental spondylotic changes when EMG findings extend beyond the cervical cord.
Do not start chronic immunosuppression (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange) for ALS — there is no benefit and treatment delays correct diagnosis.
Do not defer respiratory assessment in a symptomatic patient — even mild FVC reduction warrants close monitoring and NIV planning.
Do not dismiss bulbar or progressive symptoms as functional / psychiatric without a complete neurological workup.
required_recommendations: Perform EMG/NCS sampling the bulbar region plus ≥2 spinal regions to document lower-motor-neuron involvement and exclude conduction block.
Obtain brain MRI to exclude structural mimics (cervical myelopathy, demyelinating disease, brainstem tumor).
Order a mimic-exclusion lab panel (CK, B12, TSH, HIV, RPR, SPEP, anti-GM1 IgM, androgen receptor CAG repeat in males).
Measure baseline respiratory function (FVC, MIP/MEP, SNIP) to inform NIV timing.
Apply Awaji-Shima 2008 / Gold Coast 2020 criteria to confirm the diagnosis.
Initiate riluzole 50 mg twice daily after baseline LFTs unless contraindicated; arrange monthly LFT monitoring for the first 3 months.
Refer to a multidisciplinary ALS clinic for SLP, dietetics, respiratory, and social-work input.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

accepted: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) concurrent with virologically suppressed HIV

differential.key_features: Reported HIV-associated ALS-like syndromes typically with uncontrolled viremia; this patient is suppressed
Predominantly UMN with sensory involvement; sensory NCS here is normal
Tenofovir and integrase inhibitors not classically associated; pattern is motor only
Brain/spine MRI excludes structural cord disease
Neurogenic EMG pattern with fasciculations excludes IBM

key_clinical_evidence: Diagnosis requires evidence of both upper-motor-neuron involvement (hyperreflexia, Babinski, Hoffman, brisk jaw jerk, spasticity) and lower-motor-neuron involvement (atrophy, fasciculations, EMG denervation) with progressive spread, while excluding mimics — Awaji 2008 / Gold Coast 2020.

EMG in bulbar plus ≥2 spinal regions documenting fibrillations, positive sharp waves, complex fasciculation potentials, and large-amplitude long-duration polyphasic MUPs with reduced recruitment satisfies the electrodiagnostic criterion.
Normal sensory NCS and absence of conduction block are pivotal: they exclude common mimics including multifocal motor neuropathy, CIDP, and Kennedy disease.
Mild-to-moderate CK elevation (2–5× ULN) is consistent with ALS and does not itself indicate a primary myopathy.
Cervical spondylotic changes on MRI are common incidental findings in the at-risk age group; bulbar findings or multi-region EMG denervation cannot be attributed to cervical disease.
Baseline FVC, MIP/MEP, and SNIP/NIF inform NIV timing — NIV initiation at FVC <50% predicted or SNIP <40 cmH₂O prolongs survival and improves quality of life.

July 2026 review applied end to end: EMG/NCS is the required ALS-specific test; brain and cord MRI and targeted labs exclude mimics; respiratory function is a recommended safety baseline; genetics is separately offered after counselling; CSF is absent except in five atypical mimic work-ups.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive arm and leg weakness over 10 months in HIV-positive patient on ART

past_medical_history: HIV positive, on antiretroviral therapy, undetectable viral load

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. T is a 46-year-old woman living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy with undetectable viral load presenting with 10-month progressive arm and leg weakness. She was diagnosed with HIV 12 years ago and has been stably treated on bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide for 3 years with consistently undetectable viral load and CD4 count >500 cells/uL.

She first noticed left arm weakness and wasting 10 months ago and was initially referred to HIV neurology given concern for HIV-related complications. However, the pattern of weakness with visible muscle twitching and fasciculations, combined with hyperreflexia and a Babinski sign, is not typical of HIV myelopathy (vacuolar myelopathy) or HIV-associated neuropathy.

Her HIV neurologist considered HIV vacuolar myelopathy, CMV radiculopathy, and lymphoma as possible etiologies. MRI spine was obtained and showed no vacuolar changes, no cord compression, no lymphoma. CD4 count 520 cells/uL argues against opportunistic CNS processes. The fasciculations in the arms and the left tongue, together with combined upper and lower motor neuron signs, prompted further neurological evaluation.
